pool.prompt: A 144-fiber OSP trunk cable uses which primary construction type?
choices: Tight-buffer (each fiber individually coated to 900 um)
Loose-tube (fibers float in gel or dry-block buffer tubes)
Figure-8 (fiber + messenger integrated in one jacket)
Rollable ribbon only (no loose-tube option exists at 144F)
pool.explanation: Loose-tube is the dominant OSP trunk cable construction. Fibers float freely in oversize buffer tubes, protecting them from tensile and thermal stress across the outdoor temperature range. Tight-buffer is primarily for indoor/premises use.
pool.citation: FOA Reference Guide to OSP design; ICEA S-87-640.

pool.prompt: Match each cable construction type to its key advantage.

items.label: Thermal and tensile protection for outdoor runs
Direct fiber termination without fanout kit
Mass-fusion splicing of 12 fibers per cycle
High fiber density with rollable handling

pool.explanation: Loose-tube: thermal/tensile slack protects OSP fibers. Tight-buffer: 900 um OD allows direct termination. Ribbon: mass-fusion splicing is roughly 12x faster per fiber on high-count cables. Rollable ribbon: combines ribbon density with easier tube coiling.

pool.prompt: In a loose-tube cable, why is the buffer tube's inner diameter intentionally larger than the fiber bundle it contains?
choices: To reduce manufacturing cost by using less precise tubing
To allow the fibers slack room to move freely when the cable contracts in cold weather or bends during installation, preventing tensile stress on the glass
To make room for future fiber additions inside the same tube
Larger tubes are required by NEC fire code regardless of function
pool.explanation: The intentional oversize of the buffer tube — whether filled with gel or dry-block SAP tape — is the defining feature of loose-tube construction. It lets fibers move freely without being stressed when the cable experiences thermal contraction or bending.

pool.prompt: You are specifying cable for a 288-fiber feeder route where rapid splice closure is the highest priority. Which construction type provides the greatest splicing speed advantage?
choices: Loose-tube with gel-filled buffer tubes
Tight-buffer breakout cable
Ribbon or rollable ribbon with mass-fusion splicing
Figure-8 self-supporting cable
pool.explanation: Ribbon and rollable ribbon enable mass-fusion splicing — roughly 12 fibers per splicer cycle. For 288 fibers: about 24 ribbon cycles vs. 288 individual cycles with loose fiber, a difference of hours at a single splice closure.

pool.prompt: What is the primary reason tight-buffer construction is used indoors/premises rather than for OSP trunk cable?
choices: Tight-buffer cable is significantly cheaper than loose-tube for any application

Tight-buffer's 900 um individually-coated fibers allow direct termination without a fanout kit, which suits shorter indoor runs — but lacks the thermal/tensile slack protection loose-tube provides for the wider temperature swings and mechanical stress of outdoor OSP routes
Tight-buffer cannot carry more than 12 fibers
Tight-buffer is not compatible with fusion splicing
pool.explanation: Tight-buffer's advantage (direct termination convenience) trades off against the protective slack that loose-tube construction provides — a tradeoff that favors tight-buffer indoors (controlled environment, shorter runs) and loose-tube outdoors (temperature extremes, longer runs, tensile stress).

pool.prompt: What does rollable ribbon construction combine that neither traditional flat ribbon nor loose-tube achieves alone?
choices: The lowest possible cost of any fiber construction type
High fiber density with mass-fusion splicing speed, while retaining handling flexibility closer to loose individual fibers (rather than a rigid flat ribbon stack)
Immunity to all bend-radius restrictions
The ability to eliminate buffer tubes entirely
pool.explanation: Rollable ribbon is designed to combine ribbon's mass-fusion-splicing speed advantage with more flexible, rollable handling inside the buffer tube than a rigid flat ribbon stack — packing more fiber density while easing installation handling.

pool.prompt: A splicer opens a 432-fiber cable and finds a mix of loose individually-colored fibers rather than ribbons. What does this construction choice cost them, relative to a ribbon cable of the same fiber count?
choices: Nothing — splice time is identical regardless of construction
Significantly more splice time, since each fiber must be individually fusion-spliced rather than splicing 12 fibers per mass-fusion cycle
The loose-fiber construction is actually faster to splice than ribbon
Loose fiber construction cannot be spliced at all above 144 fibers
pool.explanation: Without ribbon's mass-fusion capability, each of the 432 fibers requires an individual splice cycle — a substantial time cost compared to the roughly 36 mass-fusion cycles (432/12) a ribbon cable of the same count would require.

pool.prompt: Why does OSP trunk cable predominantly use loose-tube rather than tight-buffer construction, given that tight-buffer allows faster termination?
choices: Tight-buffer cable cannot be manufactured above 24 fibers

Termination convenience matters less for trunk cable (which is mostly spliced, not directly terminated) than surviving decades of outdoor thermal cycling and tensile stress — loose-tube's slack design protects against exactly those OSP-specific stresses
Loose-tube is required by NEC fire code for all outdoor cable
Tight-buffer fiber has fundamentally different optical properties than loose-tube fiber
pool.explanation: OSP trunk cable is predominantly spliced at distribution points rather than directly terminated fiber-by-fiber, so tight-buffer's termination-speed advantage matters less than loose-tube's protection against the outdoor stresses (temperature extremes, tension) that trunk cable must survive for decades.
